positions/house-church-movement/oneLine: Christians can and often should gather as small, lay-led congregations in homes, as in the New Testament, especially under persecution or as an alternative to institutional churches.
positions/house-church-movement/coreClai: The New Testament church met in houses (Rom 16:5; Philemon 2); the home is a legitimate full church.
Every member participates; leadership is plural and largely lay.
Under hostile governments, unregistered house churches preserve faith and obedience to Christ over the state.
Small groups multiply rapidly and foster discipleship.
positions/house-church-movement/origin: In China, after the founding of the state-supervised Three-Self Patriotic Movement (1954), leaders such as Wang Mingdao and Watchman Nee refused to join and were imprisoned; during the Cultural Revolution (1966–76) all public worship ceased and faith survived in homes, growing rapidly after 1979 into large networks (e.g. in Henan and Wenzhou). Iranian house churches grew after 1979. In the West, the British "house church movement" of the 1970s (later New Churches) and later "simple" or "organic" church networks (Wolfgang Simson, Frank Viola) drew on the same model.
positions/house-church-movement/proponen: Wang Yi (Early Rain Covenant Church, sentenced 2019)
positions/house-church-movement/stronges: It follows the New Testament pattern and has proved extraordinarily resilient and fruitful under persecution.
It enables participation of all believers and costs little, suiting poor and persecuted contexts.
It protects the Church’s freedom from state control.
Critics argue that lack of trained leadership and accountability can foster heresy or cult-like groups (e.g. Eastern Lightning in China, which mainstream house churches reject).
Registered (Three-Self) Christians and some observers argue that registration allows legal stability and open witness.
In the West, critics see "organic church" polemic against institutions as ignoring the historic Church’s wisdom.
positions/house-church-movement/response: House-church networks have developed training, confessions (e.g. the 1998 Confession of Faith of Chinese house-church leaders) and inter-network accountability.
They argue that state registration often involves unacceptable compromises on teaching and evangelism of minors.
positions/house-church-movement/conseque: Made China home to one of the world’s largest Christian populations (Pew 2011 estimated about 67 million Christians in China; estimates vary widely).
Provoked recurrent crackdowns (e.g. 2018 regulations, closures of Shouwang and Early Rain churches).
positions/emerging-progressive-christian: Christianity must be re-expressed for a postmodern, pluralist culture: less certainty and boundary-keeping, more conversation, community, justice and inclusion, sometimes with revision of traditional doctrines.
Faith is a journey and conversation, not a closed system of propositions; doubt is welcome.
Following Jesus means embodying the kingdom of God in justice, peace and care for creation.
Church should be missional, contextual and participatory (house churches, pubs, ancient-future liturgy).
Progressive forms revise traditional teaching on hell, atonement, Scripture’s inerrancy and sexuality (full LGBTQ inclusion).

The emerging church arose among younger evangelicals in the US, UK and Australia around 1995–2005: Brian McLaren (A New Kind of Christian, 2001), Emergent Village, Tony Jones, Doug Pagitt, the UK’s alternative worship and Fresh Expressions (Anglican–Methodist, 2004). Progressive Christianity draws also on older liberal traditions (Marcus Borg, John Shelby Spong) and popular authors such as Rob Bell (Love Wins, 2011) and Nadia Bolz-Weber.
It speaks to people alienated by rigid, politicised or consumerist church cultures.
It recovers neglected emphases: the kingdom, justice, creation care, contemplative practice and ancient liturgy.
It models humility in a pluralist world.

Evangelical critics (D. A. Carson, Becoming Conversant with the Emerging Church, 2005; DeYoung and Kluck, Why We’re Not Emergent, 2008) argue it undermines truth claims and the authority of Scripture.
Critics note that progressive revisions often reproduce older liberalism, which historically led to decline.
Catholic and Orthodox critics regard it as another fragmentation of Protestant individualism.
Advocates reply that they seek a "generous orthodoxy" and that questioning is a form of faithfulness.
Fresh Expressions shows that missional innovation can occur within traditional churches without doctrinal revision.
The emerging brand largely dissolved by the mid-2010s, but its practices (missional communities, ancient-future worship) spread widely.
Progressive Christianity became a visible pole in denominational splits over sexuality.
positions/deconstruction/oneLine: A widespread, largely Western and post-evangelical process of critically re-examining inherited beliefs and church culture, which may end in reconstructed faith, a different tradition or leaving Christianity.
positions/deconstruction/coreClaims/0: Inherited beliefs and practices should be examined honestly rather than accepted on authority.
positions/deconstruction/coreClaims/1: Harm done by church cultures (abuse, authoritarianism, purity culture, racism, political partisanship) must be named.
positions/deconstruction/coreClaims/2: Faith can survive and be renewed by questioning ("deconstruct to reconstruct"), though some conclude otherwise.
positions/deconstruction/coreClaims/3: Personal experience and testimony are important sources of insight.
positions/deconstruction/keyTexts/3: Jeremiah 1:10 ("to pull down ... to build, and to plant")
positions/deconstruction/origin: The term (borrowed loosely from Jacques Derrida) became popular around 2016–2021 through social media (the #exvangelical hashtag, 2016), podcasts and memoirs (Rachel Held Evans; Josh Harris’ public renunciation in 2019). Drivers include church abuse scandals (e.g. the Mars Hill podcast, 2021; the Southern Baptist Guidepost report, 2022), the politicisation of American evangelicalism, sexuality debates and purity culture. Data show US Christian affiliation falling from about 78% (2007) to about 62% (2023–24), though the decline appeared to level off (Pew 2025).
positions/deconstruction/strongestArgume: Honest examination of belief is biblical ("prove all things") and can lead to a more mature, authentic faith.
It exposes real abuses and hypocrisies that institutions had concealed.
It mirrors historic patterns of reform, protest and doubt within Christianity (the Psalms of lament, the Reformation).
positions/deconstruction/strongestObject: Critics (e.g. Alisa Childers, Another Gospel?, 2020) argue it often begins from cultural assumptions rather than Scripture and tends toward progressive revisionism or apostasy.
Some argue it is a Western, affluent phenomenon little relevant to most Christians in the Global South.
Pastors worry that online "deconstruction" culture offers critique without community or a path to rebuilding.
positions/deconstruction/responses/0: Proponents reply that most deconstruction is driven by harm, not fashion, and that churches should listen rather than dismiss.
positions/deconstruction/responses/1: Many report "reconstruction" in liturgical, Orthodox, Catholic or mainline traditions, or renewed evangelical faith, rather than unbelief.
positions/deconstruction/consequences/0: Contributed to the growth of the religiously unaffiliated ("nones") in the West.
positions/deconstruction/consequences/1: Led many evangelicals into liturgical, Anglican, Orthodox and Catholic churches.
positions/deconstruction/consequences/2: Prompted churches to address abuse, authoritarian leadership and political entanglement.
positions/general-special-revelation/one: God makes himself known in two ways: generally to all people through creation, conscience and history, and specially through his acts and words in Israel, supremely in Jesus Christ, and in Scripture.
positions/general-special-revelation/cor: Creation testifies to God’s eternal power and divinity (Romans 1:20).
Conscience shows the work of the law written on hearts (Romans 2:14-15).
General revelation leaves humans without excuse but does not by itself save.
Special revelation culminates in Christ, the Word made flesh, and is attested in Scripture.
Nature and Scripture, rightly read, cannot ultimately conflict.
positions/general-special-revelation/ori: Rooted in Scripture and the Fathers (Justin’s seeds of the Word; Augustine’s two books); systematised by medieval and Reformation theologians (Aquinas; Calvin, Institutes 1.1-6; Belgic Confession art. 2, 1561).
positions/general-special-revelation/str: It follows explicit biblical texts (Psalm 19; Romans 1).
It explains the universal religious sense and moral awareness of humanity.
It allows both evangelistic engagement with other cultures and the primacy of Christ.
Barthians argue that “general revelation” abstracts from Christ and opens the door to idolatrous natural theologies.
Some religious pluralists argue that the distinction privileges Christianity arbitrarily.
Critics ask how a revelation that only condemns can be called “revelation” at all.
positions/general-special-revelation/res: Defenders note that Romans 1 makes the knowledge real even if suppressed, and that Christ is the Logos through whom creation reveals.
Many integrate general revelation within a Christocentric frame.
positions/general-special-revelation/con: Framework for missions theology (e.g. “eternity in their hearts”), natural law ethics and science–faith dialogue.
Underlies confessional statements on Scripture’s necessity.
positions/thomist-natural-theology/oneLi: Human reason, reflecting on created things, can know with certainty that God exists and something of his nature (the “preambles of faith”), though the mysteries of faith such as the Trinity are known only by revelation.
positions/thomist-natural-theology/coreC: God’s existence can be demonstrated from effects: motion, causation, contingency, degrees of perfection and order (the five ways).
Faith and reason are distinct but cannot contradict, since both come from God.
Revelation is morally necessary even for truths reason can reach, so that all may know them easily.
Fideism and rationalism are both rejected.
positions/thomist-natural-theology/origi: Prepared by Augustine, Anselm and Islamic and Jewish philosophers (Avicenna, Maimonides); classically formulated by Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I q.2, c.1266); defined by the First Vatican Council (Dei Filius, 1870).
positions/thomist-natural-theology/stron: It honours Scripture’s claim that God is knowable from creation and the dignity of human reason.
It provides common ground for discussion with non-Christians and other religions.
It guards against both irrational fideism and autonomous rationalism.
Kant and Hume argued that the proofs overreach the limits of experience and reason.
Barth and many Protestants argue it constructs a “god of the philosophers” rather than the God of Abraham revealed in Christ.
Orthodox theologians caution that discursive proof can eclipse apophatic, experiential knowledge of God.
positions/thomist-natural-theology/respo: Thomists answer that the five ways conclude only to a first cause, later identified with the biblical God by revelation, and that Kant’s objections assume a contested epistemology.
They stress analogy: natural knowledge is real but limited and does not replace grace.
positions/thomist-natural-theology/conse: Shaped Catholic education and apologetics; reaffirmed by John Paul II’s Fides et Ratio (1998).
Revived in analytic philosophy of religion since the 1970s.
